opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one where the answer has been shifting quite a bit as the models themselves change. If you go back a few years, retrieval was almost a necessity. The models had a few thousand tokens of context, so if you wanted them to know about something specific, like your documents, a codebase, or recent events, you basically had to bolt on a retrieval system: chunk everything, embed it, find the nearest neighbors, and stuff the top results into the prompt. It worked, but it was quite brittle. The model only ever saw whatever the retriever decided was relevant, and if the retriever got it wrong, there was no recovering.

Now, with context windows in the millions of tokens, you can do something qualitatively different. You can put an entire book, or hours of video, or a large codebase directly into the context, and the model attends over all of it. What's interesting there is that the neural network itself is effectively doing the retrieval, and it's doing it in a much richer way, because it can reason across pieces of information that a simple embedding similarity search would never have connected. In some sense, long context is retrieval, just learned end to end rather than hand-engineered.

That said, I don't think retrieval goes away. I think the two become complementary at different scales. The world's information is far bigger than any context window we'll have in the near term, whether that's the whole web, a company's entire history of documents, or someone's lifetime of personal data. So you'll still want some coarse mechanism to narrow down from billions of things to millions, and then the long-context model does the fine-grained work: reading carefully, cross-referencing, reasoning. There are also practical considerations. Long context is compute-intensive, so there's a cost and latency tradeoff, and caching and retrieval help with that.

The part I find most exciting is that the boundary between the two is getting blurrier. Models are increasingly able to decide for themselves when to search, what to search for, and how to integrate what comes back, almost like tool use. So rather than a fixed pipeline where a retriever feeds a model, you get an agent that uses retrieval as one of its capabilities and uses its own context as a kind of working memory. To me, that's closer to how we operate: we don't hold everything in our heads, but we know how to go look things up and then think hard about what we found. So I'd say hybrid systems will remain, but more and more of the intelligence about how to retrieve and how to use what's retrieved will be learned by the model rather than designed by hand.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts embedding-based retrieval with putting a book in context, but does not describe representing the entire book as a single retrieval vector or explicitly compare that with word-by-word reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says retrieval and long-context processing are complementary at different scales, with the mix shaped by corpus size and compute, cost, and latency tradeoffs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one where my view has actually shifted a bit over the last couple of years.

If you'd asked me maybe three or four years ago, I think the framing was very much "retrieval is a patch." You have a model with a fixed context, it can't see everything, so you bolt on a retriever that goes and fetches the relevant chunks, you stuff them in, and the model reasons over that. And the implicit bet a lot of people made was: as context windows grow, that patch goes away. You just put everything in context and let attention do the retrieval for you, end to end.

And to some extent that has happened. When we went from thousands of tokens to millions of tokens, a whole class of problems where you'd previously have needed a RAG pipeline just... dissolved. You can put an entire codebase, or hours of video, or a very large set of documents, in context, and the model does something that is, frankly, better than what a retriever would do, because it's not retrieving by surface similarity, it's retrieving by whatever representation is useful for the actual question. The "needle in a haystack" style of retrieval, which is what most retrievers are good at, the long-context models are now extremely good at too.

But I don't think that means retrieval disappears, for a few reasons.

The first one is just scale. A million tokens, ten million tokens, sounds like a lot, and it is, but it's still a tiny fraction of the world's information, or even of what a single large organization has. So there's always going to be a layer that decides what gets into the context at all. Whether you call that retrieval, or search, or memory, there's a selection problem that doesn't go away just because the window got bigger. It just moves up a level.

The second is cost. Attention over very long contexts is not free, and even with all the clever things people do to make it cheaper, re-reading a million tokens every time you want to answer a question is a bit wasteful if ninety-nine percent of it is irrelevant. So there's a very natural division of labor: cheap, coarse retrieval to narrow things down, and then expensive, precise reasoning inside the context. I don't think that's a hack, I think that's actually the right architecture, and it's not that different from how we operate. You don't re-read your whole library to answer a question, you remember roughly where to look.

And the third, which I think is the most interesting one, is that the line between the two is getting blurry. Within the model, attention already is a form of retrieval, it's just learned and differentiable. And on the outside, the models are increasingly the ones doing the retrieval, deciding what to search for, evaluating what came back, deciding to search again. So you end up with a system where the "retriever" and the "reasoner" are kind of the same thing wearing different hats. That's the direction I find exciting: not retrieval versus long context, but models that learn when to think over what's in front of them and when to go get more.

So my honest answer is: long context eats a lot of what retrieval used to do, and that's good. But the general problem, how do you give a model access to more than it can hold at once, that's a fundamental one, and I expect it to be with us for a long time, just in a form that looks less like a separate pipeline and more like a capability of the model itself.

r001.rationale: The response compares coarse retrieval with precise reasoning in context, but does not describe representing an entire book as a single retrieval vector or contrast that with reasoning over the book word by word.

r002.rationale: It gives general reasons to combine retrieval and long-context processing, but does not clearly state that the appropriate balance depends on the use case.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very complementary. A longer context window gives the model more room to work with information, but it doesn’t necessarily solve the problem of deciding which information to bring in. You still have to find the relevant things, and there’s a cost to putting everything into the context and processing it.

Retrieval is a way to access a much larger memory selectively. The neural model can then reason over what you retrieved, connect it to other things, and perhaps decide that it needs to retrieve something else. As context windows grow, you can bring in richer material rather than having to find exactly the right little snippet.

So I wouldn’t think of this as one approach replacing the other. The interesting question is how you learn that whole process: what to keep in the model’s parameters, what to put in context, and when to go out and get more information.

r001.rationale: The response discusses selective retrieval and richer context, but does not compare representing a whole book with one retrieval vector to reasoning over it word by word in context.

r002.rationale: It raises how to divide information between model parameters, context, and retrieval, but does not say that the balance depends on the use case.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very complementary. A longer context window gives the model more room to work, but you still have to decide what to put in that context. If you have a huge collection of documents, you probably don’t want to read the whole thing every time you ask a question. Retrieval is a way of selecting the information that might matter, and then the neural model can reason over it.

What’s interesting is that the boundary can move. Something that required a separate retrieval system before might fit directly into the context now. But as we give models more context, we also give them bigger problems and more data, so the need to find relevant information doesn’t disappear.

And fitting something into the context is different from using it well. Can the model find the important detail? Can it connect two pieces of evidence that are very far apart? Those are still meaningful questions. So I would expect these approaches to evolve together, with more learning involved in deciding what to retrieve, when to retrieve it, and how to use the result.

r001.rationale: The response discusses retrieval selecting relevant information and neural models reasoning over it, but does not identify a single retrieval vector for an entire book as coarser than word-by-word reasoning in context.

r002.rationale: It says the boundary between retrieval and context can move, but does not clearly state that the appropriate balance depends on the use case.
